newsitem.title: UK: Minor metals - Interest in cobalt, vanadium firm.
newsitem.headline: Minor metals - Interest in cobalt, vanadium firm.

text.p: Trading in the minor metals continued generally slow this week, though several traders reported pockets of consumer enquiry in the cobalt market.
Elsewhere, bismuth drifted as buying interest dried up, while vanadium firmed against the backdrop of short supply.

Several traders described the cobalt market as buoyant following buying from Japan, China, Europe and the U.S., though others said the market still remained quiet amid the traditionally slow summer period.
Cobalt was seeing some interest for prompt Russian material due to the lack of fresh shipments from Russia.
Although producer Norilsk is shipping copper and nickel it is still holding back on cobalt even now that the seasonal summer floods at the port of Dudinka have abated.

Traders suggested that the reason for the lack of freely flowing Russian material was that Russian producers believe that recent prices have been pushed artificially lower in an attempt by large European merchants to price in cheap material.
"The Russian's are not to happy about the recent pricing operation and look to be holding back material until the price returns to what they believe to be a true level," one trader said.
Others were quick to dismiss this point of view saying that with the summer lull firmly gripping the market there was still enough units on the ground in Europe to satisfy consumer needs.
High grade material, used in super alloys and the aerospace industry, was said to be thin on the ground. Traders said African and North American producers were producing low amounts of material.

Cobalt traders will closely eye the developments at Falconbridge and the union representing more than 1,400 of the miner's Sudbury workers. Contract talks broke down on Wednesday after the union angrily left the bargaining table. Sudbury produced 730 tonnes of cobalt in 1996.
Bismuth drifted back as buying interest abated.
Traders said that the move lower largely reflected the slow summer months but did not expect prices to fall significantly.
"Bismuth is like a deflated souffl," one London trader commented.

One producer source agreed that prices of bismuth were on the turn but said the market should be underpinned by a lack of Mexican and Peru offers. "The only material available at the moment is from China which is generally of poor quality," the source said.
Tight supply, good demand and slow shipments from China lifted vanadium. Traders said that raw material is lacking, pointing out that New Zealand Steel will reline one of its smelters in September.
This will take around two months and will have a major impact on vanadium availabilty.
Cadmium was showing signs of moving higher as several traders believed that major producers were sold out for 1997. They noted interest from China, India and Japan.

One trader said the emergence of Japanese enquiry would help to spark an upside move. "They have (Japan) been out of the market for some time, if they are about to buy then prices will move strongly higher," the trader said.
